To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

mutation induction due to exposure to radon progeny is determined by the radiation burdens of nonprogenitor cells, that the mutagenesis is dominated by the cell cycle shortening of inactivated cells, and that the mutation rate increases with dose rate up to a threshold, beyond which the progenitor cell proliferation is enhanced.
mutation induction due to exposure to inhaled alpha radiation is dominated by radiation-induced cell cycle shortening and the mutation rate as a function dose rate exhibits a threshold.
the mutagenicity of densely ionizing alpha particles is dominated by cell inactivation and that the inverse dose-rate phenomenon is explained by progenitor cell hyperlasia.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the relationships between the cellular and the tissue levels of organization in the context of radiation mutagenesis.

the development of a model of mutation induction by inhaled alpha particles that is able to describe the effects of chronic exposure at the tissue level and to predict the effects of different exposure conditions.
the modeling of the cellular effects of ionizing radiation at the tissue level, and it provides new insights into the relationships between cellular and tissue effects of radiation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

mutation induction in the bronchial mucosa is determined by the radiation burdens of nonprogenitor and progenitor cells and that the relative importance of the two factors varies depending on dose rate.
the mutagenesis in the bronchial tissue is determined by the balance between the radiation damage to the cells and their regenerative capacity.
the dose-rate effect is a manifestation of the interplay between the radiation burden of the non-progenitor and the progenitor cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mutation induction by inhaled alpha particles can be modeled at the tissue-level by considering the cell cycle shortening effect of densely ionized tracks.

the model developed is a useful tool for predicting the tissue level effects of inhaled radon daughters and for understanding the relationships between the effects observed at the different levels of biological organization.

the model developed in this study is capable to describe the mutagenic effects of inhaled radon decay products at the tissue level and to provide a possible explanation for the observed inverse dose-rate effect.
The main takeaway from our work is that
modeling of radiation effects at the cellular level can be used to understand the mechanisms of tissue response and the dose-response relationships characteristic of different levels of organization.
the dose rate dependence of the mutation induction rate is determined by the balance between cell proliferation and cell death.

the modeling of the effects of inhaled radon and radon progeny at the tissue level is a promising approach to understand the biological responses of the bronchus to radiation and to interpret the epidemiological data.
